trap.wrong: "Build the platform up front so every team can reuse it."
trap.why: A platform built before the use cases are understood encodes the wrong abstractions, and teams work around it.
trap.probe: The rule of three, a stable interface, a team that owns it as a product, adoption by pull.
trap.say: "Build it once, adapt it the second time, extract a platform the third time, owned by a team that treats it as a product."

thesis: Build a platform when several teams need the same capability, the interface has stabilised, and the cost of everyone building it separately is clear. Otherwise ship the one-off and extract a platform later from real, repeated usage.
pitch: Platforms are tempting because they promise reuse, but a platform built before you understand the use cases encodes the wrong abstractions and then every team works around it. My rule of thumb: the first time, build it for the one use case; the second time, copy and adapt and notice what changed; the third time, you understand the variation well enough to extract a platform. I'd also check that the interface has stabilised, that there's a team willing to own it as a product with support, documentation and roadmap, and that the cost of duplication, such as divergent security, operational load and inconsistent behaviour, is real. When building a platform, start from the existing implementations, keep the first version narrow, make the easy path the default, and measure adoption and satisfaction rather than mandating it.

points.d: Extract a shared capability after it's been built and adapted several times, when you can see what really varies.
If requirements still change monthly, a platform will churn its users. Wait until the shape settles.
Security fixes applied in five places, inconsistent behaviour customers notice, five on-call burdens. Without real cost, duplication may be fine.

points.h: A team that owns it as a product
points.d: Platforms need roadmaps, docs, support, versioning and migration help. Without an owner they decay.
Base the platform on existing implementations rather than designing from scratch, and migrate those users first.
Cover the common 80% well; leave escape hatches for the rest rather than trying to handle every case.
Make it the easiest option. Measure adoption and user satisfaction; mandates hide a bad product.

decision: One-off first; extract when three or more teams need it, the interface is stable, duplication costs are measurable, and an owning team exists.
numbers: Break-even sketch: if a capability costs each team 4 engineer-weeks to build and 1 week/quarter to maintain, a platform costing 12 weeks plus 2 weeks/quarter pays off once 3–4 teams use it.
pitfalls: Building a platform for one team's use case and calling it general.
No owner, so the platform's bugs block every team.
Over-general abstractions that make the common case hard.
Forcing adoption before the platform is better than the alternatives.

followups.q: How do you handle teams with needs the platform doesn't cover?
followups.a: Provide extension points or let them build outside the platform, then fold common patterns back in.
If a managed service covers the need, use it and build only thin glue; build internally only for what's specific to you.

followups.q: How do you measure platform success?
followups.a: Adoption, time for a new team to onboard, incidents caused, and developer satisfaction surveys.

example: Three teams had built their own notification sending, each with different retry logic and provider integrations. A small team extracted a notification service from the best implementation, migrated the three teams over a quarter, and new teams adopted it voluntarily because it was faster than building their own.

sources.title: Martin Fowler: What I talk about when I talk about platforms
